messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samuel, a 65-year-old African American man who had worked for years in retail, described the storm that broke his life apart as if it were still unfolding. During a hurricane, he had been in a store when the lights failed, the wind tore at the building, and water surged in so quickly that people had to scramble for higher ground and try to find the nearest way out. What stayed with him most was the helplessness of watching familiar aisles become dangerous in minutes, of not knowing whether the exit would remain usable, and of hearing panic rise around him as the weather became violent and the room felt trapped. Since then, Samuel has been certain that the world is a dangerous place and that he has permanently changed for the worse. He spoke of himself as someone who no longer had the luxury of relaxing, because he must be on guard all the time if he wants to stay alive.

Those beliefs shape the way Samuel moves through everyday life. At work in the retail store, he makes sure to stay close to the exit and checks the surrounding aisles and doorways almost automatically, as though he is quietly mapping every possible way out before he can let himself focus on customers or stock. In any building, he scans for exits as soon as he enters, and he said that he sleeps poorly because he needs to stay alert even at night. He distracts himself with something else when he can, but the effort is not casual; it is his way of trying to keep fear from taking over. Yet the more he positions himself near doors, keeps his eyes moving across a room, and stays mentally busy, the more he feels that danger is close by, as if his own precautions confirm that something bad could happen at any moment. Those habits also leave him feeling even more convinced that he has been altered by the disaster, because life now seems organized around protecting himself from a world that cannot be trusted.

The memories remain equally forceful. Samuel described them as a film that plays over and over, and when a siren sounds, rain lashes a window, or he hears people talking urgently in the store, the memory does not feel like something completed in the past. It feels like it is happening right now, with the same pressure in his chest and the same sense of being back inside that storm-darkened building. He said that when he remembers the frightening event, it is not like recalling a story; it is as if the scene is present again, immediate and physical. Those moments of reliving strengthen his sense that the danger is still here, and they feed the belief that he has never really recovered from the event. In turn, that feeling of being back there makes him scan harder, stay closer to exits, and keep looking over his shoulder, because he trusts the memory more than reassurance. He notices that the more he tries to manage the fear by watching the room, the less settled he feels, and the more he interprets his own ongoing alertness as proof that the world remains threatening and that he himself has been changed in some lasting way.

Over months, Samuel’s routines have narrowed. He is more likely to linger near the store entrance than walk the floor freely, and he has withdrawn from situations that leave him feeling boxed in. At home, his wife has noticed that he is difficult to settle at bedtime and that he is always listening, always checking, as though rest itself might be unsafe. What brought him to seek help was the accumulation of this strain and the fear that he would spend the rest of his life trapped in the storm’s aftermath. He is most afraid that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will happen before he can react, yet he is also hoping that treatment might help him sleep, move through the world without constant scanning, and believe again that the future is not ruled by the disaster that still feels so present to him.
